title: Le Chatelier's principle
examples: Teacher, if I increase the temperature, does the reaction shift right or left?
What happens to the equilibrium position if I add more reactant?
Can you explain why changing the pressure affects the position?

explain.say: Le Chatelier's principle helps us predict changes in equilibrium.

items: It shifts to counteract the change.
This is a key concept in chemistry.

explain.say: First, we look at the effect of changing temperature on equilibrium.
Next, we examine how changing the pressure affects the equilibrium position.
Finally, we consider the effect of changing the concentration of reactants or products.

items: Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right.
Removing a product shifts equilibrium to the right.
These changes favor the side with more substance.

explain.say: Consider the reaction for nitrogen and hydrogen making ammonia gas.
If we increase the temperature, the equilibrium will shift to the right.

faq.q: Does Le Chatelier's principle only work with gases?
faq.a: No, it applies to any reversible reaction at equilibrium. However, changes in pressure are most noticeable when gases are involved because gas volumes are affected by pressure.
asks: Does it need gas for pressure changes?
Is it only for gas reactions?

faq.q: If I change the concentration, does the equilibrium shift?
faq.a: Yes, changing the concentration of any substance will cause a shift. The system will try to use up what you added or replace what you took away.
asks: Does concentration change affect the balance?
What if I add more reactant?

faq.q: Does temperature change affect the equilibrium constant?
faq.a: Yes, changing the temperature actually changes the value of the equilibrium constant, K. This is a more advanced concept than just shifting the position.
asks: Is K constant regardless of T?

faq.q: What is the difference between a stress and a shift?
faq.a: The stress is the external change you apply, like adding heat. The shift is the system's response to counteract that initial stress.

faq.q: Why must the reaction be at equilibrium for this principle to work?
faq.a: The principle describes how a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance. If it is not at equilibrium, there is no established balance to resist the change.
asks: Can I use this if it's not balanced?
Does it need to be at rest?

faq.q: If I change the pressure, does the reaction always shift?
faq.a: No, if the number of moles of gas on both sides is equal, changing the pressure will not cause a shift in the equilibrium position.
asks: If moles are equal, what happens?
Does pressure change always cause a shift?

faq.q: Is the effect of heat the same as the effect of temperature?
faq.a: No, heat is the energy transferred, which causes the temperature change. We use the heat change, delta H, to determine if the reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
asks: Is heat the same as temperature?
How do I know if it's endo or exo?

facts: Equilibrium is a state where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
Increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction of the reaction.
A change in pressure only shifts the equilibrium if the number of moles of gas differs between reactants and products.
Changing concentration moves the system away from the original equilibrium position.

quiz.say: For the reaction A + B ⇌ C, what happens if you increase the concentration of A?

options.show: The equilibrium shifts to the right.
options.say: The equilibrium shifts to the right.

options.show: The equilibrium shifts to the left.
options.say: The equilibrium shifts to the left.

quiz.why: Adding a reactant (A) increases its concentration, so the system shifts right to use up the added reactant and re-establish balance.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the system must respond to the added stress to return to a new balance.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because the reaction continues, but at a new, shifted balance point.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might think the system overcompensates by favoring the reactants.

quiz.say: If a reaction has fewer moles of gas on the product side, what happens when pressure increases?

options.show: The equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.
options.say: The equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.

options.show: The equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.
options.say: The equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.

quiz.why: Increasing pressure favors the side that takes up less space, which is the side with fewer moles of gas.

wrong.0: This is wrong because pressure changes are a form of stress that the system must counteract.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the reaction continues, just at a new equilibrium position.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because high pressure compresses the system, favoring the smaller volume side.

quiz.say: Which change will cause the equilibrium to shift to the left for the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃?
quiz.why: The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature favors the exothermic reaction, shifting the balance to the left.

wrong.0: This is wrong because adding a product always shifts the equilibrium in the reverse direction, which is left.
wrong.1: This is wrong because adding heat favors the endothermic direction, which is the forward reaction, shifting it right.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the product side has fewer moles of gas, so pressure increases shift it right.
